5. The CHT consisting of three districts, namely, Rangamati, Bandarban and Khagrachari covers a total area of 5,138 square miles which is one-tenth of the total territorial area of Bangladesh and is home to a population of about 10 Lac which constitutes 0.5% of the total population of Bangladesh. Topographically, the CHT is a distinctly hilly area dotted by valleys. An understanding of the history of the civil and political administration of the area now known as the CHT takes one back to the 18th century when in 1760 the then Mughal Governor of the province of Bengal transferred the then District of Chittagong to the British East India Company. A century later in 1860, the British colonial government formed the Chittagong Hill District comprising of the eastern hilly areas of the then Chittagong District. In 1900 important and far reaching changes in the administration of the Hill Tracts were made by the British Government by enacting the Chittagong Hill Tracts regulation 1900 (Regulation No. 1 of 1900) (hereinafter interchangeably referred to as the "CHT Regulation 1900" or the "Regulation") and by 'framing Rules there under. The Regulation, the Rules and Orders of the CHT came to be collectively known as the 'Hill Tracts Manual' in accordance with the provisions of which the CHT continued to be administered. 

 6. Pursuant to the Hill Tracts Manual the CHT came to be divided into three circles, namely, the Chakma Circle with headquarters at Rangamati, the Bomang Circle with headquarters at Bandarban, and the Mong Circle with headquarters at Manik Chari in Khagrachari. The head of the Circle is known as the Chief, popularly known as the 'Raja' or 'King'. These Circle Chiefs or Kings have always had a distinctive role to play in the administration of the CHT notwithstanding that the administration was formally run by the Deputy Commissioners and Sub-divisional Deputy Commissioners. Notably, though the CHT fell within the boundaries of the undivided province of Bengal, its administration by different law as reflected in the Hill Tracts Manual led it to acquire the status of a 'Non-regulated District'. 

 7. By section 5 read with section 46(1) of the Government of India Act 1935, ("the 1935 Act") Bengal was a Governor's province in the Federation of India. Section 91(1) of the 1935 Act empowered the King by Order in Council to declare certain areas as "excluded area" and "partially excluded area." By section 2, read with Part I of the Schedule to the Government of India (Excluded and Partially Excluded Areas) Order 1936, the 'Chittagong Hill Tracts' under the province of Bengal was specified as an excluded area. By section 92 of the 1935 Act, though the executive authority of a province extended to excluded and partially excluded areas, the provision nevertheless was against the application of any Act of the Federal or Provincial Legislature, "to an excluded or partially excluded area unless the Governor by public notification so directs." 

 8. The Indian Independence Act 1947, ("the 1947 Act"), enacted by the British Parliament on 18 July 1947 and creating the two independent dominions namely India and Pakistan with effect from 15 August 1947, by section 2 specified the territories of the two dominions. Accordingly, by operation of section 3 of the 1947 Act the province of Bengal as constituted under the 1935 Act ceased to exist, and two new provinces known as East Bengal and West Bengal were constituted. It is to be noted that in the First Schedule to the 1947 Act, which provisionally included the Bengal districts in the new province of East Bengal, the Chittagong Hill District was conspicuously absent. Such absence finds meaning and substance in the provisions of section 8 of the 1947 Act, by virtue of which the 1935 Act continued, with necessary amendments, to be the Constitution of Pakistan until March 1956 when the first Constitution of Pakistan was framed. Consequently, by operation of section 5 read with sections 46(1), 91 and 92 of the amended Government of India Act 1935 (as amended by the Constituent Assembly of Pakistan from time to time) the position of the CHT as an excluded area in the province of East Bengal remained unaltered. 

 (d) A constitutional provision restricting the amendment of the CHT Regulation 1900, and imposing a ban on Bengali settlement in the CHT. It is averred that these demands were rejected outright by the Prime Minister who, on the contrary, argued for relinquishing such parochial and ethnic aspirations in favour of these being subsumed under a broader notion of nationalism to facilitate national integration. 

 12. This Court notes that subsequent developments in the CHT and the political positioning of the PCJSS along with the Shanti Bahini vis-a-vis successive governments came to be greatly informed by the taxonomy of citizen-ship as adopted in the 1972 Constitution in reinforcement of the unitary character of the new State. The Constitution as adopted in November 1972 having termed every citizen as "Bangalee" (Bengali), MN Larma could be said to have drawn the battle lines very early on in 1972 when he vehemently opposed on the floors of the Constituent Assembly the lumping together of the Chakma people with Bengalis in blatant disregard of the Chakmas' separate identity. The seed of the unitarily of the State so sown in the Constitution is perhaps nowhere better manifested than in the Bengali immigration into the CHT in the following decades. A succinct account of the various phases of such migration considered in their larger historical context is found in Devasish Roy's chapter entitled "The Discordant Accord: Challenges In The Implementation of the Chittagong Hill Tracts Accord of 1997" in "Implementing Negotiated Agreements: The Real Challenge to Intrastate peace," edited by Miek Boltjes at pages 115-146 (TMC Asser Press, the Haque, Netherlands, 2007) Mr Roy writes accordingly at pages 121-122: 

 "Bengali in-migration into the CHT had started during the nineteenth century, but even after the departure of the British in 1947, the settlers name up less than 10 percent of the population. This was to rise to almost 50 percent in 1991, making the indigenous people a near-minority in their ancestral homeland. The internal immigration policies of the different governments were not the same. The British government had allowed limited immigration into the CHT in order to facilitate trade and irrigation-oriented intensive agriculture, both the which were relatively new to the indigenous peoples. It was careful not to allow large-scale immigration, fearing the growth of anti-British sentiments, which were more common in the plains of Bengal. The Pakistani government's role (1947-1971) regarding immigration was more ambivalent, while the role of successive Bangladeshi administrations on this issue has varied from covert encouragement (early 1970s) to a directly sponsored population transfer programme (1979 to 1984). The transmigration of the largely Muslim peasants from various lowland districts led to the displacement of tens of thousands of indigenous people, thereby partly civilianizing the ongoing conflict and adding ethnic and religious overtones to a conflict that was hitherto largely restricted to the non-Muslim indigenous guerrillas and predominantly Muslim Bengali government security forces. Of course, that does not mean that innocent civilians, whether Bengali or indigenous, were not victimized earlier, but at least their number until then was not so visibly large. This part-civil part-military conflict continued up to the 1990s and it was not until the signing of the 1997 Accord that the organized internal war formally ended. In the meantime, thousands of lives had been lost, tens or thousands of people rendered homeless, and an untold number had to suffer the indignities of rape, torture and imprisonment. Although there were casualties on both sides of the ethnic divide, the indigenous people suffered the most because the balance of force was not on their side, among other things. Moreover, the security forces had, on the whole, paid little heed towards the human rights of the indigenous people in their quest to contain the insurgency." 

 13. It is against the backdrop of such a "part-civil part-military conflict" in the CHT that on 6 March 1989 three identical laws, namely Rangamati Hill District Local Government Council Act 1989 (Act No. 19 of 1989) Khagrachari Hill District Local Government Council Act 1989 (Act No. 20 of 1989) and Bandarban Hill District Local Government Council Act 1989 (Act No. 21 of 1989) (hereinafter collectively referred to as "the Original Acts of 1989" as necessary) were passed by Parliament by which local governments were established in the three Hill Districts under Article 59 of the Constitution. These laws made detailed provisions for the establishment and functioning of local governments by the elected representatives of the people consisting of both the tribal people and Bengali settlers. The political context, necessity and objective of these three pieces of legislation is explained in Moudud Ahmed's book titled "South Asia: Crisis of Development—The Case of Bangladesh" (The University Press Limited, Dhaka 2002) at pages 64-65 thus: 

 iv. 	Section 28 of the Impugned Acts Nos.  9 and 10 and section 27 of the Impugned Act No. 11 as amends section 62 of the Original Acts by which permanent preference has been ensured in the Police Service for the tribal people, such preference being discriminatory against the Bengali settlers, therefore, violates the guarantees under Articles 27 and 29 of the Constitution. 

 23. The political context of these two Applications in the terms of what this Court perceives to be the political vicissitudes of the tribunal peoples is best introduced by the following excerpts from the Memoirs of the former Chakma Chief, Raja Tridiv Roy entitled "The departed Melody" (PPA Publications, Islamabad, Pakistan, July 2003) that provides an account of the post-1972 political developments bearing upon the CHT, the resultant conflict and the need to a political settlement as embodied in the Peace Accord. Raja Tridiv Roy appears to emphasize that Bengali nationalism in all its manifestations as informed post 1971 State formation and nation building by its very ethos remained so very exclusionary of other identities that the tribal peoples of CHT got political short-changed and became constitutional outcasts. In a chapter entitled "Traumas of the Chakmas", Raja Tridiv Roy writes thus at pages 330-331: 

 "Mahfuzul Hoque in "Ethnic Insurgency and National Integration" writes on page 80, "Misunderstanding between the Bangladesh Government and the tribal people arose immediately after independence. Bengali Freedom Fighters killed tribal people of Khagrachari, Dighinala and Barkal." And on page 81, "Widespread repression and atrocities during Mujib regime were committed by Rakkhi Bahini [paramilitary security force of the post-independent government] against the tribal people. And again he says, "At a rally at Rangamati Sheikh Mujib declared that all tribal people would be known as Bengali and would have no other identity." 

 During Pakistan days there was no government sponsored induction or infiltration by plainsmen. Mahfuzul Haque in "Ethnic Insurgency and National Integration," says: "In mid-1979 late President Ziaur Rahman took decision to settle land-less families in the sparsely populated areas of the hills. The decision was construed by the tribal leaders as a government attempt to change population pattern of the hills. In February, 1980, truckloads of poor Bengali families mainly from northern Bangladesh poured into the Hill Tracts. They were attracted by the government scheme to provide five acres of hilly laud, four acres of mixed lands, and 2.5 acres of paddy land for each newly settled Bengali family." 

 ii.	Health : Except the Chakma, the Other tribes' access to sanitary latrine is very low compared to the Bengali population 50% of Bengalis have access to latrine compared to 29% Marma, 10.8% Tripura, 13.2% Bawm, 9.1% Mro, and 8.0% Tanchangya. Knowledge about symptoms of diarrhoea is 68% amongst the Bengali population compared to 65% in indigenous people. Only 34% of the indigenous population knows how to prepare oral re-hydration saline compared to 65% of Bengali people. Knowledge about vaccination of children is 37.7% in the Bengali population, compared to 22.2% indigenous people. In case of pregnancy care, only 9.5% indigenous people get antenatal care compared to 29.2% of Bengalis. 73.6% of Bengalis receive immunization during pregnancy, which is only 37.9% in case of indigenous people 8.2% Bengalis have postnatal care, compared to only 3% indigenous people. 

 iii.	Safe Drinking Water: Compared to 60% of Bengali people, only 36% of indigenous peoples in CHT use tubewell as source of drinking water. Only 33% of indigenous people use tube well as the source of cooking water compared to 42% Bengalis. In terms of adequate sources of drinking water the percentages among the Bengali and indigenous people are respectively 54% and 51%. 

 iv.	Electrification: About 91% indigenous households and 73% Bengali house-holds are deprived of electricity. 

 v.	Communication: The CHT tribes live in the remoter areas of the CHT compared to their Bengali counterparts. More than 10% of all Unions in the CHT (all situated in Baghaichhari, Juraichhari, Rowangchhari, Ruma and Thanchi thanas) are not accessible otherwise than by a travel on foot taking one or two days walking from the nearest road or riverside. These Unions are almost exclusively populated by the indigenous people. 

 29. It is in this context that it is noted that much of what was anticipated and stipulated in the multi-dimensional, multilayered Peace Accord has been translated into legislative action producing the four piece of impugned legislation. In this Court's view these Impugned Acts more aptly constitute the subject matter of judicial scrutiny. There are other provisions in the intricately stranded Peace Accord that are admittedly in the process of being implemented. Upon a consideration of the same it is evident that certain administrative, political and legal pathways are yet to evolve or be followed to fully implement these provisions. The pursuit of those pathways, particularly with regard to the effective functioning of the Land Commission, as are yet to be fully developed are not ripe understandably for constitutional scrutiny. The Peace Accord in this sense in indicative of future courses of action over and beyond the fulfillment of its primary objective of securing a political resolution to a politico-military conflict. Again, a resolution of the conflict itself, this Court finds, has inevitably led to an exhaustion of the Peace Accord's essential political substratum. It is in that overall context that we have considered the argument on behalf of the Respondent Regional Council by learned Advocate Dr. Kamal Hossain that the Peace Accord not amenable to a constitutional analysis adopting a strict constructionist approach. To the extent that the immediate political objectives of the Pea Ce Accord have been satisfied it is the Court's view that the Peace Accord does not indeed permit a judicial review at this point in time that is not to say, however, that political act are not per se amenable to judicial scrutiny. They are indeed so subject to such scrutiny should they involve constitutional is shall be seen the impugned legislation stemming from that Peace Accord and with which the relevant provisions of the Peace Accord can be said to have otherwise merged have indeed been accepted by this Court for independent judicial inspection below. This Court is also not inclined to accept the argument of the Respondents that since the laws in question were passed in 1998, that is subsequent to the Peace Accord and, since no government has proceeded on the premise that this is an unconstitutional Accord as evident in the absence of any issue to that effect having ever been raised in Parliament since 1997, and six successive governments having not repealed the Peace Accord, such delay and acceptance over a protracted period would obviate a judicial scrutiny of the Accord. That fact that such an argument is inherently misconceived is borne out by the judgment in the Italian Marble Case commonly known as the 5th Amendment Case reported in 2006 (Special Issue) BLT in which the 5the Amendment 1979 to the Constitution was revisited years later by the High Court Division as per a challenge made in December 2000 and the Rule made absolute in 2005. There are, however, certain features fundamental and unique to the Peace Accord itself that in this Court's perception takes it out of the fold of the constitutional scheme as we understand it. That Court has probed into this aspect in relation to the issue of the constitutionality of the execution of the Peace Accord raised by the Petitioner in both Writ Petitions. This Court in accepting the fact of political exigency that informed the adoption of a particular manner of execution of that Peace Accord notes that such mode of execution was informed in turn to a large extent of the parties' understanding of what was being executed. This Court is of the view that the Peace Accord is fundamentally an intrastate political pact that marks the cessation of hostilities between belligerents. At its core the multistanded Peace Accord is actually a 'Treaty of Peace' that proceeds beyond a mere truce and a mere true and aims at a permanent end to an insurgency based on commitments of sustainable peace. The Black's Law Dictionary defines such a 'treaty' to be an agreement of a contract made by belligerent powers, in which they agree to lay down their arms, and by which they stipulate the conditions of peace and regulate the manner in which it is to be restored and supported. In this Court's opinion, there is no better way to describe the Peace Accord. That being the case, the Peace Accord does not in this Court's opinion neatly fall into the category of Article 145 contracts and deeds or indeed Article 145A international treaties. It is clearly not a treaty as not being entered into between independent entities or communities having the right of self-government on account of one party to the Peace Accord, that is, the PCJSS not possessing such right of self-government. Though clearly not creating any obligation under international law the Peace Accord has on the other hand given rise to commitments. But stretching the interpretation of the Peace Accord has on the other hand given rise to commitments. But stretching the interpretation of the Peace Accord beyond that to bring it within the purview of Article 145 becomes problematic because Article 145 primarily deals with contracts or bids reflecting a bargain struck for consideration. That objective of Articles 145, that is somewhat latent in the formulation of the Article in the Constitution, becomes clear upon a perusal of the corresponding Article 299(1) of the Constitution of India which expressly refers to "contracts and all assurances of property" made in the exercise of the power derived from the President. It is evident that Article 299(1) of the Indian Constitution and Article 145(1) of the Constitution have been enacted primarily to guard against avoidable and unwelcome demands made on the treasury pursuant to commercial transactions, the Indian Supreme Court in West Bengal vs BK Mondal & Sons reported in AIR 1962 (SC) 779 held that Article 299(1) of the Indian Constitution has been incorporated on the ground of public policy to protect the state from the liability to unauthorized contracts and, therefore, its provisions are mandatory and non-compliance with its requirements renders a contract invalid and unenforceable. Even so, Mr Mahmudul Islam in his book "Constitutional Law of Bangladesh" (Second Edition: Mullick Brothers, Dhaka 2003) in discussing the ratio on the West Bengal Case in conjunction with Article 145 compliance measures finds, the India Supreme Court's view "too rigid" as it "goes beyond the necessity of protecting the public interest". The better view, according to Mr Islam is that expounded by the Privy Council in Montreal Street Railway Co vs Normandin reported in AIR 1917 PC. 142 that strict compliance in such cases is not to be mandatory and is to be forgone in favour of substantial compliance especially if a strict compliance test declaring a contract null and void would operate to the prejudice of all and sundry. This Court finds that if, therefore, the rigidity of the application of the Article 145(1) conditions are relaxed with regards to contracts and deeds clearly falling under the said Article's purview, there is no reason why a stricter test of validity should be applied to the Peace Accord which, in this Court's view, does not answer to the description of an Article 145(1) contract or deed in the first place. This Court, therefore, notes that when an argument of substantial compliance with the requirements of Article 145(1) can be made with regard to contracts and deeds clearly envisaged in the said Article, the Petitioners in both the Writ Petitions have not satisfactorily explained why the same provisions should be found to be of mandatory application with regard to the Peace Accord which, in our view, is not an Article 145(1) contract: or deed. This Court, therefore, finds that the multi-dimensional Peace Accord does not permit of a neat categorization under the Constitution. Being an essential link in a long-standing and ongoing political process this intrastate peace pact between belligerents is not strictly contemplated for in our Constitution and must, therefore, be found to be indeterminable as to its nature and validity by reference to the Constitution. It is here that we find the relevance of and the merit in Dr Kamal Hossain's submission that the Constitution indeed lacks in process formulation and the CHT peace process with the Peace Accord as its vital component, therefore, considered on their own do not indeed permit a constitution-al analysis adopting a strict constructionist approach. In a similar vein Mr Devasish Roy appearing for the Respondent Regional Council has argued to this Court's satisfaction that the CHT Peace Accord is neither an executive deed nor a contract within the meaning of Article 145, but is merely a political document agreement setting out the political goodwill between the NCCHT negotiating on behalf of the Government and the PCJSS representatives of the tribal people to bring an end to the armed hostility in the CHT. It is further submitted that it is in that spirit of political engagement and accommodation that the Peace Accord was negotiated and executed by the then Chief Whip Mr Abul Hasnat Abdullah in 1997, it always being the intention of both parties concerned to accept him as representing the Government of Bangladesh in that exercise.
